design_detail: Uncontrolled phase 1/2 open-label treatment-development trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172, named in the Acknowledgments; MAPS protocol MPVA-1) of MDMA-facilitated cognitive-behavioural conjoint therapy (CBCT) for PTSD in six heterosexual couples in which one partner had chronic PTSD: a condensed version of the 15-session CBCT protocol delivered over 7 weeks, with two all-day sessions in which both partners took MDMA, two co-therapists (one expert in MDMA therapy, one in CBCT), and assessments before, at mid-treatment, after treatment and at 3 and 6 months; growth-curve models and within-group effect sizes. Brief report (no Results subsections beyond two). The setting is not stated here; the companion paper on secondary outcomes from the same six couples (Wagner et al., 2021) gives a private practice clinic in Charleston, South Carolina. Funded by MAPS. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest, and the card uses ROBINS-I as the batch brief directs for non-randomized intervention studies.
can_establish: That MDMA could be given to both members of six couples within a condensed course of CBCT without serious adverse events or dropouts, and what happened to PTSD symptoms, depression, sleep and relationship satisfaction in these 12 people over 6 months.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA added anything to CBCT, an established therapy that improves PTSD on its own (there is no CBCT-alone or placebo arm); whether any change is due to the treatment rather than natural course, regression to the mean or expectation; rare harms; or effects in couples other than White, heterosexual, mostly relationally satisfied couples treated by the developers of the therapy.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: One partner with current PTSD on the CAPS-5 for at least 6 months; both partners at least 18, generally healthy, proficient in English, willing to stay off psychiatric medicines during the study, to follow food, drink and nicotine restrictions before MDMA sessions, to use birth control if able to become pregnant, to be video-recorded and not to join other trials. Excluded: acute psychosis, acute mania, substance use disorder, pregnancy or nursing, weight under 48 kg (Method › 1.1 Participants, 1st paragraph). The companion paper adds no active suicidal planning or intent and no severe partner aggression, and specifies no current substance use disorder (Wagner et al., 2021).
sample.demographics: Mean age about 47 (patients 47.1, SD 12.5; partners 46.6, SD 11.2); all White ('Caucasian'); all heterosexual couples; 4 of 6 patients men; 5 of 6 patients with multiple traumas (index trauma childhood sexual abuse 3, childhood physical abuse or neglect 2, adult combat 1); all patients with comorbid diagnoses and earlier drug and psychological treatment; 3 of 6 patients in current psychotherapy; at baseline 2 patients and 3 partners relationally distressed (Couples Satisfaction Index below 104.5) (Method › 1.1 Participants, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: All six couples completed the protocol; there were no missing clinician PTSD interviews; across the other self-report measures and occasions 86% of assessments were completed (2. Results, 1st paragraph; Method › 1.3 Assessment, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Couples willing to take MDMA together, to stop psychiatric medicines and to be video-recorded, treated by the developers of the therapy and of MDMA-assisted therapy; all White and heterosexual; most patients had long histories of treatment. Expectations were probably high and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to all: CBCT sessions 1 to 3 in person the day before the first MDMA session, sessions 4 and 5 on the morning of it, the MDMA session (6 to 8 hours) and an integration session the next morning; sessions 6 to 9 by secure video over 2.5 weeks; sessions 10 and 11 the day before the second MDMA session, then the second MDMA session and an integration session; sessions 12 to 15 weekly by video; 7 weeks in all. MDMA sessions were timed to follow the communication-skills work and to fall in the middle of the cognitive work (Method › 1.2 Treatment, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: each partner took 75 mg MDMA in the first session and 100 mg in the second, with an optional supplemental half-dose 1.5 hours later in both sessions; participants were told the supplement could prolong the therapeutic window (Method › 1.2 Treatment, 2nd paragraph). The companion paper gives the supplements as 37.5 mg and 50 mg (Wagner et al., 2021).
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorder was an exclusion criterion, yet Table 1 lists a substance use disorder among SCID-5 diagnoses in 3 of 6 patients and 1 partner, without saying whether these are past diagnoses (Table 1; reporting issues). Other drug use during the study is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; psychiatric medicines were stopped for the study.

comparison.controls: None: within-person change from pre-treatment to mid-treatment, post-treatment and 3- and 6-month follow-ups.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; without a comparison group, the effect of CBCT itself, the natural course, regression to the mean and expectation cannot be separated from any effect of MDMA.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: CAPS-5 (clinician-rated, by independent assessors trained to reliability); PCL-5, patient and partner versions; Couples Satisfaction Index (CSI), with its overall relationship-happiness item also given at each visit. Secondary: BDI-II, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (reappraisal and suppression), Trauma and Attachment Belief Scale (TABS). SCID-5 at baseline. Adverse events from enrolment to treatment completion and at 3 and 6 months; spontaneously reported experiences and listed effects on session days and contact days (Method › 1.2 Treatment, 2nd paragraph; 1.3 Assessment, 1st to 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated measures; relational distress defined as a CSI total below 104.5 (Table 1 footnote).
outcomes.operationalization: Change over time in growth-curve models with log-transformed days since baseline, fixed slopes and random intercepts; within-group Cohen's d from pre-treatment to each time point, computed on the models' estimated means and the raw pooled SDs (Method › 1.4 Analyses).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Twelve outcome models (CAPS-5, patient and partner PCL-5, BDI-II, PSQI, two ERQ subscales, TABS, patient and partner CSI, patient and partner relationship happiness) (Table 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None possible: every participant received MDMA, and the independent CAPS-5 assessors knew it; the self- and partner-reports come from people who had taken MDMA. Two authors (Monson and Wagner) were paid to provide the treatment (COI Statements).

analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172: actual start 3 July 2016, first submitted 16 August 2016, posted 23 August 2016 (about six weeks after the start). Registered primary outcome: CAPS-5 total severity at the primary endpoint (visit 16, about 2 months) and its change from baseline; PCL-5 (patient and partner), CSI, BDI-II, PSQI, TABS and ERQ are registered as secondary outcomes, whereas the article calls PCL-5 and CSI primary self-report outcomes. Results posted 19 July 2021 (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: The adverse-event and reaction tables are in two supplementary Word files, not read because they are downloads; the article names only the most common reactions. The registry's adverse-event list (5% threshold) was read instead.
analysis.power: No power calculation; a treatment-development pilot of six couples.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six couples given a condensed course of an established couple therapy for PTSD with two MDMA sessions for both partners, clinician-rated PTSD fell from about 41 to 19 after treatment and 16 at 6 months (model estimates), five of six patients no longer met PTSD criteria, depression, sleep and relationship satisfaction improved, all couples finished, and no serious adverse event was reported. With no comparison arm none of this can be attributed to MDMA rather than to CBCT, time or expectation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says MDMA "holds promise as a facilitator of CBCT to achieve more robust and broad effects" (Abstract). The Discussion says the combination may potentiate the treatment effects, that its effect sizes were greater than those of individual MDMA-assisted therapy (citing the pooled phase 2 analysis that PMC marks as retracted) and on par with or greater than CBCT alone, and that the largest effects at 6 months suggest MDMA facilitation may confer ongoing benefits (Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs): comparisons of within-group effects in six people with other studies' results. The Discussion itself calls these comparisons tentative, and the Limitations say the lack of randomization or control severely limits the conclusions (Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).

timeline.event: Wagner, Mithoefer, Mithoefer & Monson, J Psychoactive Drugs: a case example of the combined treatment (cited in this report; not read).
This report: primary outcomes of the six-couple uncontrolled trial.
Wagner et al., Front Psychiatry: relational and growth outcomes from the same six couples (not independent).

replication.where_it_stands: One uncontrolled trial of six couples, reported in two papers by the same team. The project's evidence map lists a pilot of a brief MDMA-enhanced CBCT (Morland et al., 2026; read by this reader, card sc_morland_2026) and a registered randomized trial of conjoint therapy with and without MDMA (NCT06044675, recruiting); no controlled result exists in the sources read.

funding.funder: Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS), grant MPVA-1 (Funding Statement; Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Dr Monson receives book royalties from Guilford Press for the treatment manual of interest to this study; Drs Monson and Wagner received payment from MAPS for providing treatment in the study; Dr and Ms Mithoefer receive payments from MAPS PBC for work in medical affairs, training and supervision, and from Awakn Life Sciences as members of its Scientific Advisory Board; Drs Feduccia and Jerome were paid by MAPS PBC as employees for work related to this study; Dr Yazar-Klosinski is a salaried MAPS employee paid for work related to this study; Dr Doblin is paid by MAPS as Executive Director; Dr Liebman has no conflicts (COI Statements).
funding.affiliations_note: The first author developed CBCT and receives royalties on its manual, and she and the second author delivered the treatment; five authors are MAPS or MAPS PBC staff. Data are openly available on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/7fuwd) (Data sharing statement); not inspected here.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of CBCT with MDMA against CBCT with an active placebo, in couples with PTSD from more diverse backgrounds, with therapists other than the developers, blinded independent assessors, measured expectancy and follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: No comparison group, and the treatment includes a full course of CBCT, which the authors describe as efficacious on its own; any contribution of MDMA cannot be separated from CBCT, time, regression to the mean or expectation.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Self-selected couples willing to take MDMA together, most relationally satisfied at baseline; recruitment is not described.
All received the same protocolized treatment.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Three of six patients were in current psychotherapy at baseline (Table 1) and the report does not say whether this continued; doses of the optional supplements taken are not reported.
No missing clinician interviews; 86% completion of the other self-reports.
Outcomes rated by participants and partners who had taken MDMA, and by assessors who knew everyone had; the therapists include the first two authors, one of whom developed the therapy.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Registered about six weeks after the start; PCL-5 and CSI, registered as secondary, are presented as primary; the registered CAPS-5 endpoint is reported, but the registry's posted endpoint mean (16.3) differs from the article's estimated mean (19.37).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that MDMA adds to CBCT, the study is at critical risk of bias: it has no comparison arm, and the therapy it adds MDMA to is itself an efficacious treatment. Unblinded self-, partner- and assessor-ratings add serious concerns. The paper can be cited for feasibility (all six couples completed), for the absence of serious adverse events in 12 people, and for the observed changes as a description; it cannot be cited for MDMA's contribution or for comparisons with other treatments.

key_findings.finding: Six heterosexual couples (12 people), one partner in each with PTSD; mean age about 47; all White; 4 of 6 patients men; all patients with comorbid diagnoses and earlier treatment; 2 patients and 3 partners relationally distressed at baseline.

All couples completed the protocol and there were no serious adverse events; the most common reactions after MDMA sessions in patients and partners were diminished appetite, anxiety, headache and jaw tightness (counts only in the supplementary tables, not read).

Clinician-assessed PTSD (CAPS-5, estimated means): 41.42 (SD 5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after, 17.43 (17.14) at 3 months and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months; growth-model B = −4.64, P < .001; within-group d 2.10, 1.88 and 2.25. All but one patient had a sustained remission of the clinician-assessed PTSD diagnosis.
key_findings.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
key_findings.note: Editors' check: d = 2.10 equals the change of 22.05 divided by the root mean square of the two SDs (10.52).

key_findings.finding: Self-rated PTSD (PCL-5): 62.64 (6.35) to 23.96 after treatment and 17.20 at 6 months, B = −8.14, P < .001, d 2.72 to 3.59; partner-rated PTSD: 49.58 (8.52) to 21.54 and 16.64, B = −5.90, P < .001, d 1.85 to 2.72.
key_findings.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Patient depression (BDI-II) 32.91 (8.75) to 12.75 after treatment and 9.23 at 6 months, B = −4.24, d 1.50 to 2.53; sleep (PSQI) 14.24 (3.54) to 10.37 and 9.69, B = −0.81, P < .01, d 0.88 to 1.18; emotion regulation, reappraisal B = 1.38 and suppression B = −1.12, both P < .01; trauma-related beliefs (TABS) B = −12.01, P < .01, d 0.98 to 1.17.
key_findings.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Relationship satisfaction (CSI): patients 105.37 (13.39) to 127.00 after treatment and 130.78 at 6 months, B = 4.55, P < .05, d 0.82 to 1.22; partners 98.10 (50.81) to 125.34 and 130.10, B = 5.73, P < .05, d 0.64 to 0.80. Both relationally distressed patients were satisfied after treatment; one patient satisfied at baseline was dissatisfied afterwards (the one who kept the PTSD diagnosis); one of three distressed partners stayed distressed (that patient's partner). Relationship happiness: patients B = 0.35, partners B = 0.33, both P < .001.
key_findings.locator: 2. Results › 2.2 Intimate relationship outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Registry results: CAPS-5 at the primary endpoint 16.3 (SD 13.71) and change from baseline −25.7 (13.89), n = 6. Adverse events (5% threshold): every patient and every partner had at least one non-serious event from enrolment to 2 months after the last MDMA session (for example nausea, decreased appetite and fatigue in 2 patients each; anxiety in 1 patient and 1 partner), 2 patients and 2 partners in the 6-month follow-up period; no serious events or deaths; the list includes a spontaneous abortion in one partner during the follow-up period, entered as non-serious.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172 (API v2) › Results › Outcome Measures; Adverse Events

key_findings.finding: Registration: NCT02876172, actual start 3 July 2016, first submitted 16 August 2016; primary outcome CAPS-5 at the primary endpoint (about 2 months) and its change; PCL-5, CSI, BDI-II, PSQI, TABS and ERQ registered as secondary outcomes; results posted 19 July 2021.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures

key_findings.finding: Limitations as stated: no randomization or control condition, which severely limits the conclusions; expert therapists in each modality, which limits generalizability; too small to examine moderators or mechanisms; a phase 2 randomized trial is being prepared.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentages that six people cannot produce: Table 1 gives 4 male patients as 60% (4 of 6 is 66.7%) and depressive and anxiety disorders in 4 partners as 60%; the text says 60% of patients had received trauma-focused therapy and 40% dialectical behaviour or cognitive-behavioural therapy; the text says 50% of partners had a mental health condition, while Table 1 lists a depressive disorder in 4 of 6 partners.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample description is internally inconsistent; cite counts, not percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: Substance use disorder was an exclusion criterion, but Table 1 lists it among SCID-5 diagnoses in 3 of 6 patients and 1 partner (and anorexia nervosa in one of each), without saying whether these are past diagnoses; the companion paper specifies no current substance use disorder.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably lifetime diagnoses, but the report does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: Three of six patients were in current psychotherapy at baseline (Table 1); the report does not say whether it continued during the trial.

The text gives the ERQ suppression effect as d = 1.12 to 1.20 at post-treatment and follow-ups, but Table 3 gives 0.91 at post-treatment; the BDI-II slope (B = −4.24) has no P value; the Discussion compares 'd = .82' for patients with 'g = .64' for partners.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (2. Results › 2.1, 2nd paragraph; Table 3; 3. Discussion, 2nd paragraph)

reporting_issues.issue: The registry's posted CAPS-5 endpoint mean is 16.3 (SD 13.71), while Table 2 gives an estimated post-treatment mean of 19.37 with the same SD; for every secondary outcome the registry's posted means equal the article's 'estimated means' to two decimals (for example PSQI 14.24 and 10.37; BDI-II 32.91 and 12.75).
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Results › Outcome Measures); PMC HTML (Table 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which values are observed and which model-estimated; the within-group effect sizes depend on which they are.

reporting_issues.issue: PCL-5 and the Couples Satisfaction Index, registered as secondary outcomes, are called primary self-report outcomes in the article; registration followed the actual start by about six weeks.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Method › 1.3 Assessment, 2nd paragraph); registry record (Outcome Measures; Status)

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's benchmark for individual MDMA-assisted therapy (a pooled pre–post effect of about d = 1.20) and its statement that MDMA has been studied with individual therapy for PTSD rest on the pooled phase 2 analysis (Mithoefer et al., 2019), which PMC's reference list marks as retracted.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (3. Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; References)

reporting_issues.issue: The article reports no adverse event by name beyond the most common reactions; the registry's list includes a spontaneous abortion in one partner during the follow-up period, recorded as non-serious.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Adverse Events); PMC HTML (2. Results, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Safety statements should be read with the registry's list; neither source allows a judgment of relatedness.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7748057 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3, figure legend, funding, conflicts and data statement), read in this reader's own browser tab; ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT02876172 (API v2) for registration, outcomes and posted results including adverse events; the Crossref record for the DOI. The two supplementary Word files (adverse events and reactions) were not read because they are downloads; Fig. 1 values were not extracted.
